blocks.text: The three pillars make one case. Demand work fills seats only if the seats exist, supply work pays only if the product can be booked, and both need the enabling base to last.

The growth model sets out three paths from the 2025 base of 1,498,829 arrivals: 1,822,634 in 2035 on the conservative path, 2,175,778 on the base path and 2,516,282 on the accelerated path (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20). The deck is explicit that the paths differ by intervention, not by demand potential (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p19). Each step up the case therefore rests on a set of moves, and the table below maps each set to the focus areas that deliver it.

blocks.caption: Growth paths and their interventions

blocks.message: Each step of the growth case rests on a named set of interventions, and each set draws on focus areas in all three pillars.

blocks.text: **The gateway binds first, at peak.** The growth model draws current air access as a line at 1.8 million inbound seats, and the base case crosses it at the 2030 year point (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). Relief at Cape Town International arrives about 2032 for the international terminal and about 2033 for the runway (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p103). ACSA now schedules the realigned runway for December 2029, subject to contract award. This plan keeps about 2033 as its planning date and treats the earlier date as upside (ACSA, Q1 2026/27 presentation to the Portfolio Committee on Transport, as reported by Travel News, Aug 2026). Between those dates, growth has to come from larger aircraft and added frequency on the full routes, from hub-carrier capacity and, for domestic connections, from George, whose terminal doubles by 2028 or 2029 (focus areas 5, 6 and 7).

The deck draws arrivals and seats against one axis and prints no seat table behind the 1.8 million line. The crossing year is read from the chart: after the 2028 point (1,673,855) and by the 2030 point (1,802,929).

**If the supply moves slip, the case stops at the seat line.** The deck states that the projected growth cannot be realised without additional capacity or frequency (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21), and that without confirmed routes the accelerated case reverts to base (p20). On the full routes, demand work cannot make up the gap, because marketing raises fares rather than seats (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, In Conclusion); on the hub routes, which have seats to spare, it can.

**Below the gateway, the pillars depend on each other.** Green-season demand needs seats in the months carriers now cut (focus areas 2 and 7). Dispersal needs product that can be booked and reached (focus areas 3, 9 and 10). Inclusion needs a seller and a safe visit before exposure (focus areas 13 and 19). Every target needs data that today sits with SA Tourism, ACSA and the booking platforms (focus area 18).

**Air access and bookability move first, because every other lever runs through them.** The table below sets the order. Chapter 4 turns it into eighteen initiatives with owners, phases and decision gates.
